guide.title: Sant'Eustachio, Rome: Borromini's Sant'Ivo, the Caravaggios of San Luigi dei Francesi and the Senate's palaces
guide.intro: Sant'Eustachio is R. VIII, the eighth of Rome's rioni by toponymic code, and it is a long, narrow strip of the historic centre with a stag's head for its emblem. Borromini's church of Sant'Ivo stands in the courtyard of the Palazzo della Sapienza, seat of Rome's university until 1935 and of the State Archive since 1936. The Senate sits in Palazzo Madama, and the Constitution of the Italian Republic was signed in the library room of Palazzo Giustiniani on 27 December 1947. Three Caravaggios hang in the Contarelli chapel of San Luigi dei Francesi and a fourth in Sant'Agostino, on the same pillar as a Raphael. Two working theatres, the Argentina and the Valle, have published 2026/2027 seasons. Eight further churches serve the French, Belgian, Romanian, Piedmontese, Norcian and Baptist communities of Rome. Nearly every edge of the rione is a street shared with a neighbour.

sections.heading: The rione and its borders
sections.body:
The rione is roughly 900 metres from north to south and about 250 metres across, and it touches seven neighbours. it.wikipedia's article on the rione gives Roma Capitale's border description: via dei Portoghesi, via della Stelletta and piazza e via di Campo Marzio with Campo Marzio; via e piazza della Maddalena, via del Pantheon and piazza della Rotonda with Colonna; via della Rotonda, piazza Santa Chiara, via di Torre Argentina and largo di Torre Argentina with Pigna; largo Arenula, via di Sant'Elena, via in Publicolis and via di Santa Maria del Pianto with Sant'Angelo; via Arenula, piazza Benedetto Cairoli and via dei Giubbonari with Regola; via dei Chiavari, piazza dei Satiri, largo Pallaro, largo dei Chiavari, corso Rinascimento and piazza delle Cinque Lune with Parione; and piazza Sant'Agostino and via dei Pianellari with Ponte.

At Largo di Torre Argentina the Teatro Argentina is in Sant'Eustachio; the Area Sacra with its four Republican temples, the Curia di Pompeo and the Torre del Papito are in Pigna, and the sources name different rioni for the square itself. Corso del Rinascimento, cut through this quarter in the 1930s, is the line between Parione and Sant'Eustachio, and Palazzo Madama, the Palazzo della Sapienza and Palazzo Baldinotti Carpegna all carry addresses on it. The church of Santa Maria in Publicolis, which a map may put on this side of the line, stands in Sant'Angelo on it.wikipedia's own statement that it is in that rione. Piazza Benedetto Cairoli is in Regola, while the church of Santi Biagio e Carlo ai Catinari addressed on it is in Sant'Eustachio, because Roma Capitale says in its own words that the church sorge nel rione Sant'Eustachio.

One name causes confusion and is not a boundary problem at all. Roma Capitale heads its page Basilica di Sant'Agostino in Campo Marzio; Campo Marzio there is the ancient region of the city, not Rione IV, and the basilica, its piazza and the Biblioteca Angelica in the convent block are all in Sant'Eustachio.

sections.heading: The Sapienza block, the national churches and two theatres
sections.body:
The spine of the rione is the block bounded by Corso del Rinascimento, via degli Staderari and piazza Sant'Eustachio. The Palazzo della Sapienza held the Studium Urbis, the university Boniface VIII founded in 1303, until 1935; the Archivio di Stato di Roma has been in it since 1936, with the Biblioteca Alessandrina's hall of 1659 to 1665 now used for exhibitions. Borromini's Sant'Ivo alla Sapienza stands in the courtyard, and the rector's office states that the church is closed for works in progress, so a visitor arriving today sees the spiral lantern from the street and not the interior. In the flank wall on via degli Staderari, Pietro Lombardi's Fontana dei Libri of 1927 carries the rione's stag between four antique books, inscribed S. EVSTACCHIO with the rione numeral R IV, which Roma Capitale points out is wrong: Sant'Eustachio is the eighth rione.

Five churches here belong to communities from outside Rome, and they are the reason the rione's church-going hours are so uneven. San Luigi dei Francesi is the French national church; San Giuliano dei Fiamminghi is the royal Belgian church, whose vault carries the arms of Bruges, Ghent and Ypres and a Glory of St Julian frescoed by William Kent; San Salvatore alle Coppelle is the national church of Romania, with an iconostasis and the Eastern rite; the Santissimo Sudario dei Piemontesi was built by Piedmontese, Niçois and Savoyards and is now a subsidiary church of the Ordinariato Militare in Italia; and Santi Benedetto e Scolastica all'Argentina is the church of the nursini, the people of Norcia. The Chiesa evangelica battista on via del Teatro Valle was inaugurated with a service on Sunday 2 November 1878.

The two theatres both work. The Teatro Argentina, which stands in front of the Area Sacra, opened on 13 January 1732 with Domenico Sarro's Berenice and is the Teatro di Roma's main house. The Teatro Valle, inaugurated on 7 January 1727 and named for Franca Valeri in 2021, reopened in part in 2018 after a closure and an occupation, and Teatro di Roma programmes it.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
No source states a metro station or a bus route for Sant'Eustachio, and no walking times or distances are given either. Steer by street numbers instead, and remember that several of them sit on streets that are rione boundaries.

Roma Capitale gives Corso del Rinascimento 40 for the Palazzo della Sapienza and for the church of Sant'Ivo alla Sapienza, whose Sunday entrance during the works is Via del Teatro Valle 33. San Luigi dei Francesi is at Piazza di San Luigi de' Francesi 5, Sant'Agostino at Piazza di Sant'Agostino 80 and the Biblioteca Angelica at Piazza di Sant'Agostino 8. Palazzo Giustiniani is at Via della Dogana Vecchia 29 and Palazzo Madama on Piazza Madama. The rione's title church is at Via di Sant'Eustachio 19, and the Palazzetto di Tizio da Spoleto at Piazza di Sant'Eustachio 6, on the same square. Sant'Andrea della Valle is addressed at Piazza Vidoni 6, with the Abate Luigi statue at the corner of that square. Via del Sudario holds three buildings in a row: the Palazzetto del Burcardo at 44, the Santissimo Sudario dei Piemontesi at 47 and San Giuliano dei Fiamminghi, which the church gives as 41 and Roma Capitale as 40. The Teatro Argentina is at Largo di Torre Argentina 52 and the Teatro Valle at Via del Teatro Valle 21.

One address needs a warning. Roma Capitale places Palazzo Patrizi Montoro on Piazza di San Luigi de' Francesi, while its address field gives a street in another rione, so no street number for that palace is given here.

faq.question: Can I go into Borromini's Sant'Ivo alla Sapienza?
faq.answer: Not at present. The rector's office states that the church is closed for works in progress. The Sunday 11.00 Mass is held in the Sala della Rettoria, entrance Via del Teatro Valle 33, from September to June and not in July or August, and Roma Capitale states that a Mass is celebrated Monday to Friday at 9.00 in the same room. The lobed dome and the spiral cusped lantern, with their travertine torches and the wrought-iron sphere, cross and dove, are visible from outside the Palazzo della Sapienza.

faq.question: Where are the Caravaggios?
faq.answer: Three of them are in the Cappella Contarelli, the last chapel on the left in San Luigi dei Francesi: the Vocazione di san Matteo, San Matteo e l'angelo and the Martirio di san Matteo, painted between 1599 and 1602. A fourth, the Madonna dei Pellegrini of 1604, is in the first chapel on the left in Sant'Agostino, in the same church as Raphael's fresco of the Prophet Isaiah of 1512 and two Sansovino marbles. Roma Capitale directs enquiries about Mass times and visiting at San Luigi dei Francesi to the church itself, so no hours are given here; for Sant'Agostino it publishes Mass on Monday to Saturday at 08.00 and 18.30 and on Sundays and feasts at 08.00, 10.00, 12.00 and 18.30, with its own caveat that times may change.

faq.question: Can I visit Palazzo Madama, the seat of the Senate?
faq.answer: Roma Capitale states that visits to Palazzo Madama are suspended. Palazzo Giustiniani, where President Enrico De Nicola signed the Constitution of the Italian Republic on 27 December 1947 in the library room, is the residence of the President of the Senate; no source states any visiting arrangement for it, so none is given here. Palazzo Baldinotti Carpegna, joined to Palazzo Madama by a two-storey portico, houses Senate offices and standing committees.

faq.question: Is the Area Sacra di Largo Argentina in this rione?
faq.answer: No. The sunken archaeological enclosure with its four Republican temples, the Curia di Pompeo and the Torre del Papito is in Pigna, and the sources name different rioni for the square around it. What Sant'Eustachio holds at that address is the Teatro Argentina, which stands in front of the Area Sacra, and the Palazzetto del Burcardo on via del Sudario, whose absorbed tower gave the largo its name.

faq.question: Which places in Sant'Eustachio state opening or Mass times?
faq.answer: Sant'Andrea della Valle's own site gives Monday to Saturday 15.00 to 19.30 and Sunday 08.30 to 19.30; San Giuliano dei Fiamminghi states that it is open for prayer and visits Monday to Thursday, 10.00 to 12.00; Roma Capitale publishes Mass times for Sant'Agostino, the Santissimo Sudario dei Piemontesi, Santi Benedetto e Scolastica and Santi Biagio e Carlo ai Catinari. No source states hours for the basilica of Sant'Eustachio, the Archivio di Stato, the Biblioteca Angelica or the palaces.

faq.question: What is the Abate Luigi?
faq.answer: A late-Roman statue of a togate man, headless, standing at the corner of piazza Vidoni against the flank of Sant'Andrea della Valle. It is one of Rome's talking statues, the Congresso degli Arguti, with Marforio, Babuino, Facchino, Madama Lucrezia and Pasquino, and it has stood in its present place since 1924. Roma Capitale sites both the statue and piazza Vidoni in the rione Sant'Eustachio.

photos.title: Sant'Ivo alla Sapienza: the dome and spiral lantern
photos.description: The lobed dome and spiral cusped lantern Borromini raised over the church of Sant'Ivo alla Sapienza, seen above the concave facade in the courtyard of the Palazzo della Sapienza.
photos.author: Paolo Villa

places.name: Chiesa di Sant'Ivo alla Sapienza
places.summary: Francesco Borromini's church, standing in the courtyard of the Palazzo della Sapienza. The rector's office states that the church is closed for works in progress. The Sunday 11.00 Mass is held in the Sala della Rettoria, entrance Via del Teatro Valle 33, from September to June and not in July or August. Roma Capitale states that a Mass is celebrated Monday to Friday at 9.00 in the same room.
places.history: Urban VIII appointed Borromini architect of the Sapienza in 1632, to finish a complex already designed and partly built by Giacomo Della Porta; the church's own site dates the building to 1642 to 1660. Borromini added the attic over the existing facade, carrying the eight-pointed stars and six hills of the Chigi for Alexander VII, and above it the lobed dome and the spiral cusped lantern with travertine torches, topped by a flaming crown with a wrought-iron sphere, cross and dove. The plan is centralised on a six-pointed star. Pietro da Cortona painted the high-altar canvas of Sant'Ivo, finished in 1683 by his pupil Giovanni Ventura Borghesi, and Borromini designed the marble intarsia floor.

places.name: Palazzo della Sapienza and the Archivio di Stato di Roma
places.summary: The palace of the Studium Urbis, the university Boniface VIII founded in 1303, which stayed here until 1935; the Archivio di Stato di Roma has occupied it since 1936. Borromini's church of Sant'Ivo stands in its courtyard. No opening hours are given here; the Archive publishes its reading-room access rules itself.
places.history: Roma Capitale names Guidetto Guidetti, Pirro Ligorio and, for the sixteenth-century phase, Giacomo Della Porta on the building, and Borromini from 1632 to 1667. The Biblioteca Alessandrina, named for its patron Alexander VII Chigi, was built here between 1659 and 1665: a rectangular hall in three bays on the second floor, to the left of the church, with Clemente Maioli's allegorical Trionfo della religione on the central vault. The Archive has turned that monumental hall into an exhibition room. Its holdings run from the central administrative and judicial archives of the Papal State, from the fifteenth century to 1870, through hospital, family, confraternity and religious-corporation records and thousands of notarial protocols, to about 20,000 parchments, the earliest dated 883.

places.name: Chiesa di San Luigi dei Francesi
places.address: Piazza di San Luigi de' Francesi 5, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The French national church, which Roma Capitale describes as situata nel rione Sant'Eustachio. The Cappella Contarelli, the last chapel on the left, holds three canvases Caravaggio painted between 1599 and 1602: the Vocazione di san Matteo, San Matteo e l'angelo and the Martirio di san Matteo. Roma Capitale directs enquiries about Mass times and visiting to the church itself, so no hours are given here.
places.history: Cardinal Giulio de' Medici, later Clement VII, founded the church in 1518; Domenico Fontana completed it in 1589 to a design by Giacomo Della Porta. The travertine late-Renaissance facade has five bays and a triangular pediment carrying the arms of France, with statues of Charlemagne, Louis IX, St Clotilde and St Joan of Valois carved by Pierre Lestache in 1758. The Contarelli chapel is named for Cardinal Mathieu Cointrel, and its vault was frescoed by the Cavalier d'Arpino. The second chapel on the right, of St Cecilia, has frescoes by Domenichino and an altarpiece by Guido Reni; the organ is Joseph Merklin's, of 1881. Pauline de Beaumont, whose tomb Chateaubriand built, Cardinal de Bernis and Frederic Bastiat are buried here.

places.name: Palazzo Madama (Senato della Repubblica)
places.summary: The seat of the Senate, chosen for the Senate of the Kingdom in February 1871. Roma Capitale states that visits to Palazzo Madama are suspended.
places.history: The monks of the imperial abbey of Farfa ceded the ground in 1478 to France, for a hostel for French pilgrims. Cardinal Giovanni de' Medici, later Leo X, bought it in 1505 and had it restored to a design by Giuliano da Sangallo. It passed to Giulio de' Medici, later Clement VII, then in 1534 to Alessandro de' Medici, and on his death in 1537 in usufruct to his widow Margherita d'Austria, natural daughter of Charles V and called la Madama, from whom the palace takes its name. Paolo Marucelli finished the Baroque facade in 1642. The palace went to the Lorraine in 1737 and was bought in 1755 by Benedict XIV for the Governatorato, when a second courtyard was opened where the Senate chamber now sits; under Pius IX it housed the Ministry of Finance.

places.name: Palazzo Giustiniani
places.address: Via della Dogana Vecchia 29, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The palace where, on 27 December 1947, President Enrico De Nicola signed the Constitution of the Italian Republic, in the library room. It is the residence of the President of the Senate. No source states any visiting arrangement, so none is given here.
places.history: Roma Capitale dates the core to 1585, probably by Giovanni Fontana for Monsignor Francesco Vento, and records its purchase in 1590 by the Giustiniani, who had come to Rome from Chios after the Turkish reconquest. The palace was enlarged from 1650, in part to designs by Borromini, and its staircase and courtyard were built into the early eighteenth century, absorbing buildings as far as Piazza della Rotonda. It held the collection of sculpture and painting formed by Vincenzo Giustiniani, 1564 to 1637, which included Caravaggio, Raphael, Giorgione, Titian and Andrea del Sarto and was dispersed between the late eighteenth and the early nineteenth century. The Grande Oriente d'Italia had its seat here from 1898; the Italian State bought the building in 1943. An underground gallery built in 1938 links it to Palazzo Madama.

places.name: Basilica di Sant'Eustachio
places.summary: The church that names the rione, with a gilded stag's head carrying a cross between its antlers above the pediment. Roma Capitale gives no fixed hours for the basilica, so none are given here.
places.history: The present fabric is eighteenth-century; the surviving medieval element is the Romanesque campanile built for Celestine III around 1195 and decorated with polychrome bowls. There is a single nave with three side chapels. On the counter-facade are a Maddalena penitente window, made in the last decade of the nineteenth century by Gabriel and Louis Gesta of Toulouse, and an eighteenth-century organ. Nicola Salvi made the high altar of polychrome marble and bronze in 1739, over an urn said by tradition to hold the bodies of the saint, his wife and his children, under a baldachin with stag, dove, cherubs and palms by Ferdinando Fuga. A plaque on the facade marks a Tiber flood: AN(NO) SAL(UTIS) M VD TIBERIS SERENO AERE AD HOC - SIG(NUM) CREVIT NON(IS) DECEMB(I)R(IS) ALEX(ANDRI) VI P(ONTIFICIS) M(AXIMI) AN(NO) III, which reads 5 December 1495.

places.name: Basilica di Sant'Andrea della Valle
places.summary: A Theatine basilica under a dome Carlo Maderno raised, with Lanfranco's fresco inside it and Domenichino's on the pendentives. The basilica's own site gives opening Monday to Saturday 15.00 to 19.30 and Sunday 08.30 to 19.30; Mass on weekdays at 19.00 and on Sunday at 09.00, 11.00, 12.00 in Filipino and 19.00; confessions 30 minutes before each Mass.
places.history: Work began in 1591 to a design by Gian Francesco Grimaldi and Giacomo Della Porta, funded largely by Cardinal Alessandro Peretti di Montalto, nephew of Sixtus V. Carlo Maderno took over in 1608, widened the transept and raised the dome, which was inaugurated on 6 November 1622. Carlo Rainaldi built the travertine facade in the second half of the seventeenth century. Giovanni Lanfranco frescoed the interior of the dome between 1621 and 1625, Domenichino the pendentives and the apsidal transept between 1621 and 1628, and Mattia Preti the apse; the young Francesco Borromini worked the lantern capitals, whose cherubs' wings form volutes. The funerary monuments of Pius II, about 1470, and of Pius III Piccolomini, early 1500s, were brought here from the old basilica of St Peter's in 1614. The Barberini chapel is known as the Cappella della Tosca because part of Puccini's opera is set there.

places.name: Basilica di Sant'Agostino in Campo Marzio
places.summary: The Augustinian basilica raised above a flight of steps, holding Caravaggio's Madonna dei Pellegrini of 1604 in the first chapel on the left, Raphael's fresco of the Prophet Isaiah of 1512 on the third pillar on the left with Andrea Sansovino's marble group of St Anne with the Virgin and Child, and Sansovino's Madonna del Parto of 1516 just to the right of the entrance. The name in Campo Marzio is the ancient region's, not the rione's. Roma Capitale gives Mass on Monday to Saturday at 08.00 and 18.30 and on Sundays and feasts at 08.00, 10.00, 12.00 and 18.30, with its own caveat that times may change.
places.history: The first church here was finished in 1420 and proved both too small and too low against Tiber floods. Giacomo da Pietrasanta and Sebastiano da Firenze rebuilt it about fifty years later for Cardinal Guillaume d'Estouteville and raised it above a flight of steps; the two-order travertine facade is faced with blocks that tradition says came from the Colosseum, and d'Estouteville's arms are carved in the tympanum. Luigi Vanvitelli added the lateral volutes and, between 1746 and 1750, built the new convent and cloister, recast the interior and turned the fifteenth-century campanile into a square tower. The high altar of 1627, to a design by Bernini and executed by Orazio Torriani, carries a Byzantine Virgin and Child icon from Santa Sofia in Constantinople; Guercino and Lanfranco are in the right transept chapel. St Monica and Contessina de' Medici are buried in the church.

places.name: Teatro Argentina
places.address: Largo di Torre Argentina 52, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The main house of the Teatro di Roma, standing in front of the Area Sacra. Roma Capitale lists it as accessible, with accessible toilets, a rehearsal room and a cloakroom. The 2026/2027 season is running; tickets go through teatrodiroma.vivaticket.it and the box office numbers are 06 684000311 and 06 684000314.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the theatre opened on 13 January 1732 with Domenico Sarro's Berenice, when it belonged to the Sforza Cesarini; that Paganini played in 1827 in the room above the vestibule; and that Verdi's La battaglia di Legnano had its premiere here in 1849. The city acquired it after 1870 as its institutional theatre.

places.name: Teatro Valle "Franca Valeri"
places.address: Via del Teatro Valle 21, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A theatre of 900 seats, owned by Roma Capitale and programmed by Teatro di Roma, which took the name of Franca Valeri in 2021. Its 2026/2027 season is published and opens from 16 to 18 October with Francesco Piccolo's La sera della prima. Sei personaggi in cerca d'autore al Teatro Valle.
places.history: it.wikipedia, which records the theatre as sited in the rione Sant'Eustachio, says the nobleman Camillo Capranica financed it and Tommaso Morelli designed it, and that it was inaugurated on 7 January 1727 with Simone Falconio Prato's tragedy Matilde; it was built entirely of timber in the Italian manner, with five tiers of boxes and a gallery. Mozart's Don Giovanni had its Roman premiere here in 1811, Rossini's La Cenerentola its world premiere in 1817 and Pirandello's Sei personaggi in cerca d'autore its premiere in 1921, with works by Donizetti in between. The theatre closed in 2010, was peacefully occupied by activists from 2011 to 2014, was transferred to Roma Capitale in 2016 and reopened in part in 2018.

places.name: Biblioteca Angelica
places.summary: An Italian state library under the Ministero della Cultura, in the Augustinian convent block of Sant'Agostino. Roma Capitale counts about 200,000 volumes, among them some 3,000 Latin, Greek and Oriental manuscripts, 1,000 incunabula including the De Oratore of Cicero, 20,000 sixteenth-century editions and 10,000 prints and maps. Roma Capitale directs enquiries about access to the library itself, so no hours are given here.
places.history: Traces of a library here go back to the fourteenth century, but the decisive act was the Augustinian bishop Angelo Rocca's: in 1604 he entrusted his library of about 20,000 volumes to the friars of Sant'Agostino, endowed it, and directed that it be open to all without limit of rank or means. Lukas Holste's printed books arrived in 1661 and Cardinal Domenico Passionei's collection in 1762. By special papal authorisation the library also kept books on the Index, marked with an arrow on the spine. Luigi Vanvitelli rebuilt the reading room, completed in 1765. The Italian State acquired the library after Unification, and since 1940 the building has also housed the Accademia dell'Arcadia, founded in 1690. It has been used as a film location, including for De Sica's Il Giardino dei Finzi Contini and Howard's Angels and Demons.

places.name: Palazzo Maccarani Stati
places.summary: Giulio Romano built it in Rome between 1519 and 1524 for Cristoforo Stati, Conservatore di Roma, with the dowry of his wife Faustina Cenci. The rione's own monument list records it as Palazzo Stati Cenci alla Dogana, today Palazzo Maccarani Stati, on piazza di Sant'Eustachio. No source states any visiting arrangement, so none is given here.
places.history: The design draws on a simplified version of Bramante's Palazzo Caprini. The ground floor is rusticated, with a portal between rusticated pilasters under a triangular tympanum and four carriage doors; above it a mezzanine of four plain-framed windows, then five first-floor windows with alternating segmental and triangular pediments and five second-floor windows under flattened arches. The scheme continues on the via dei Caprettari and via del Teatro Valle elevations, and a nineteenth-century storey was added on the right. The asymmetrical courtyard has three arches on pilasters with Doric pilaster strips, an Ionic loggia above and Corinthian columns on the second level. Restorations followed in 1972 and 2001; the second uncovered painted decoration that Giuseppina Magnanimi attributed to Perin del Vaga and his shop, dated between 1543 and 1551.

places.name: Palazzo Vidoni Caffarelli
places.address: Corso Vittorio Emanuele II 116, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A palace built for the Caffarelli in 1515, and the setting of the 1536 meeting between Paul III Farnese and Charles V. Roma Capitale states that the palace houses ministerial offices, is closed to the public and can be seen only from outside.
places.history: The Caffarelli sold the palace in 1767 to Cardinal Stoppani and it passed in 1816 to Cardinal Vidoni. In 1886, after the demolitions that widened Corso Vittorio Emanuele II, the new owner Carlo Giustiniani Bandini had Francesco Settimi rebuild the elevations on the corso and on piazza Vidoni and add a storey; the original sixteenth-century facade is the one on via del Sudario. The interiors include frescoes by Anton Raphael Mengs and by the school of Perin del Vaga. Before the Second World War the building housed the directorate of the Partito Nazionale Fascista.

places.name: Abate Luigi
places.summary: One of Rome's talking statues, a late-Roman figure of a togate man, roughly life size and headless, the right arm bent with the hand on the chest and a capsa for scrolls at his feet, which dress and attribute mark as a public official. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina places him at the corner of piazza Vidoni, between Sant'Andrea della Valle and the Theatine convent, and Roma Capitale sites both the statue and the piazza in the rione Sant'Eustachio.
places.history: The Abate Luigi belongs to the group of talking statues called the Congresso degli Arguti, with Marforio, Babuino, Facchino, Madama Lucrezia and Pasquino, and popular tradition named him after a sacristan of the church of the Sudario whom the statue was said to resemble. He stood first on the corner of a small palace on via del Sudario, then in Palazzo Caffarelli Vidoni; the Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that he was moved to the courtyard of Palazzo Chigi when that building was cut back for Corso Vittorio Emanuele II, then to a niche on the Caffarelli Vidoni staircase, and has stood at piazza Vidoni since 1924. The head has been replaced repeatedly after thefts and is now missing. The base carries an inscription by Giuseppe Tomassetti, cut at the order of Prince Giustiniani Bandini: Fui dell'antica Roma un cittadino / ora Abate Luigi ognun mi chiama.

places.name: Fontana dei Libri
places.summary: A wall fountain set in a niche in the flank of the Palazzo della Sapienza: the rione's stag's head between four antique books on two brackets, with water running from two bookmark-shaped spouts and from the two upper volumes. It is inscribed S. EVSTACCHIO and the rione numeral R IV, and Roma Capitale points out that the numeral is wrong, because Sant'Eustachio is the eighth rione.
places.history: Pietro Lombardi made the fountain in 1927, within a Comune di Roma programme of fountains recalling the old rioni and vanished trades, which replaced cast-iron nasoni then thought ugly. The books refer to the university housed in the Palazzo della Sapienza, whose wall carries the fountain, and the street was once called via dell'Universita; the staderari who gave it its present name were makers of steelyard balances. Above the niche is the Medici emblem, for Palazzo Madama opposite.

places.name: Palazzetto di Tizio da Spoleto
places.summary: A small painted house on piazza di Sant'Eustachio, built at the start of the sixteenth century for Tizio di Spoleto, chamberlain to Cardinal Alessandro Farnese, later Paul III. Roma Capitale states that it can be visited only from outside.
places.history: The painted exterior is among the first independent works of Federico Zuccari, who according to Vasari got the commission through his brother Taddeo, in whose workshop he had been training since arriving in Rome in 1550. The figures show scenes from the life of St Eustace, among them the Baptism and the Martyrdom. The arms of Pius IV Medici date the work to 1559.

places.name: Palazzo Baldassini and the Istituto Luigi Sturzo
places.summary: A palace of 1515 to 1518 by Antonio da Sangallo the Younger, now the seat of a research institute with 70 personal archives, 3 party archives and a library of about 120,000 volumes. Roma Capitale records that the Istituto Luigi Sturzo was founded in 1951 by Don Luigi Sturzo and has had its seat at Palazzo Baldassini since 1956.
places.history: Sangallo built it for the jurist Melchiorre Baldassini, of Neapolitan origin, a reader in civil law at the Sapienza, consistorial advocate and advocate of the poor, who took part in the Fifth Lateran Council in 1512. The painted decoration is by the School of Raphael, with Perin del Vaga, Giovanni da Udine, Polidoro da Caravaggio and Maturino named; the Giovanni da Udine room was frescoed between 1517 and 1519, while the palace was still being built. The plan runs on an axis from the street through a vestibulum and an atrium courtyard to a viridarium at the back, behind a Florentine Renaissance facade.

places.name: Chiesa di San Salvatore alle Coppelle
places.summary: The national church of Romania, and for more than a hundred years the meeting point of the Romanian Greek-Catholic community in Rome: an iconostasis separates presbytery from nave and the liturgy follows the Eastern rite. Roma Capitale places the church in the rione Sant'Eustachio. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: Celestine III consecrated or reconsecrated the church in 1195, the date of the dedicatory plaque inside and of the small Romanesque campanile now partly absorbed into the neighbouring building. A bull of Honorius III of 1222 already calls it de Cupellis, after the workshops of the makers of small barrels, coppelle. In 1404 it was granted to the Universita degli Orefici, Ferrari e Sellari, and the saddlers stayed until 1740. From 1633 it was also the seat of the Confraternita del Santissimo Sacramento della Divina Perseveranza, which cared for sick pilgrims and foreigners: a letterbox-shaped plaque on the left flank, of the Jubilee of 1750, instructs innkeepers and lodging-house keepers to drop in a note reporting any guest who fell ill, beginning QUI DEVONO METTERE I VIGLIETTI TUTTI GLI OSTI ALBERGATORI LOCANDIERI. The medieval church was rebuilt for that Holy Year to a design by Carlo De Dominicis, funded by Cardinal Giorgio Spinola, who is buried in one of the chapels under a polychrome marble monument by Bernardino Ludovisi. Two fifteenth-century fresco fragments survive, a Dormitio Virginis and a Virgin with the Child on her knees, of the school of Antoniazzo Romano. The church has three naves, and the original marble columns were replaced by masonry piers at the end of the eighteenth century.

places.name: Chiesa di San Giuliano dei Fiamminghi
places.summary: The royal Belgian church, the national church of Belgium in Rome, administered by the Stichting Sint-Juliaan, a lay foundation descended from the old confraternity. The church gives its address as Via del Sudario 41; Roma Capitale lists it at Via del Sudario 40. The church states that it is open for prayer and visits Monday to Thursday, 10.00 to 12.00.
places.history: Tradition puts a foundation in the eighth century; more probably the Flemish community in Rome built a hospice with a chapel in the eleventh, and Robert II of Flanders, in Rome in 1096 for Urban II's crusade, is said to have stayed and restored it. The first documentary mention is 1444, the date of the statutes of the Confraternita dei Fiamminghi. Between 1680 and 1682 the confraternity enlarged the church, turning a Latin-cross plan into an oval with eight columns. The hospice closed with the French Revolution and became the Belgian college, now on via Aurelia. The small facade is set into the former hospice, with the Lion of Flanders on the portal and a modern copy of Jodocus Haerts' seventeenth-century elm statue in the upper niche, the original kept inside. The vault carries the arms of Bruges, Ghent and Ypres and a Glory of St Julian frescoed in the early eighteenth century by William Kent; Matthieu Kessels carved the monument to Ludovica de Timbrune-Valence in 1830.

places.name: Chiesa del Santissimo Sudario dei Piemontesi
places.summary: A subsidiary church of the Ordinariato Militare in Italia, which Roma Capitale describes as standing in the rione Sant'Eustachio, officiated by the Cappellani Palatini. Roma Capitale gives Mass on Monday to Friday at 16.30, on Saturday and vigils at 18.00 and on Sunday and feasts at 18.00, with its own caveat that times may change.
places.history: The origins are traced to 1270, when Piedmontese, Nicois and Savoyards returning from the Eighth Crusade formed a small community in Rome; in 1597 they founded the Confraternita del Santissimo Sudario. Under Sixtus V the archconfraternity obtained permission to build, and the church went up between 1603 and 1605 to a design by the Turin architect Carlo di Castellamonte, 1560 to 1641. Carlo Rainaldi restored it in 1678 and gave it the two-order facade, assisted by the Piedmontese painter-architect Pier Francesco Garoli. It was deconsecrated and used as a store and stables during the Roman Republic of 1798 to 1799, restored in 1856, and after 1870 served in effect as a private chapel of the House of Savoy. There is one nave with two side chapels and a polychrome stone floor; Cesare Maccari, 1840 to 1919, frescoed the vault. The high altar carries a seventeenth-century Pieta e santi by Antonio Gherardi and the left altar Il beato Amedeo IX by Giovanni Domenico Cerrini; a life-size sixteenth-century reproduction of the Shroud by Maria Francesca di Savoia was given by Clement VIII, and Lazzaro Baldi's Scene della Passione are in the sacristy.

places.name: Chiesa dei Santi Benedetto e Scolastica all'Argentina
places.summary: The regional church of the nursini, the people of Norcia, entered through the via di Torre Argentina front of Palazzo Lucarucci and recorded in the rione's own monument list. It is also called San Benedetto della ciambella. Roma Capitale gives Mass daily at 18.00, with its own caveat that times may change.
places.history: Five devotees, Laerzio Cherubini, Benedetto and Francesco Passerini, Sebastiano Masseroni and Olimpo Cistarelli, founded a company at Cherubini's house in February 1615; Paul V approved it as a confraternity on 9 November 1615 and Gregory XV raised it to a Venerable Archconfraternity on 4 February 1623. Its first official seat was a chapel inside Sant'Eustachio. In 1619 the nursino Piermatteo Lucarucci made a ground-floor room in his house available, and in 1622 left the whole building to the confraternity by will, which allowed the oratory to be enlarged into a church. The French stripped it in 1798 and the Roman Republic again in 1849, when the archive was lost; it was restored under Pius IX and Leo XIII. The archconfraternity died out in 1960 and the church passed to the Vicariate. It has no facade of its own, and the portal carries a roundel reading Divis Benedicto et Scholasticae patronis ordo et populus nursinus. The single nave, painted with false columns and inscribed Felix Nursiae tellus quae talem genuit alumnun, is divided into two bays by an arch on half-piers. The name della ciambella comes from a bronze imperial civic crown dug up in the Baths of Agrippa by Cardinal della Valle, which the diggers likened to a ring-shaped bun.

places.name: Chiesa dei Santi Biagio e Carlo ai Catinari (San Carlo ai Catinari)
places.summary: The Barnabite church built in honour of Cardinal Carlo Borromeo, which Roma Capitale states sorge nel rione Sant'Eustachio although its address is on a square in the neighbouring rione. The name ai Catinari comes from the basin-makers' shops of the quarter. Roma Capitale gives Mass on Monday to Saturday at 08.00 and on Sundays and feasts at 10.00, and states that in summer the 10.30 Sunday celebration is kept.
places.history: The Barnabites commissioned Rosato Rosati and the church was built in 1620 on the site of a small twelfth-century church. Giovanni Battista Soria built the two-order travertine facade about 1635 to 1638, its frieze cut with the name of Cardinal Leni, who paid for it. Rosati's dome, finished in 1620, rises on a tall drum with twelve pilaster strips and arched windows between them. The interior is an elongated Greek cross that took its present form in 1646 with the rebuilding of the apse, and was restored in 1897 for the canonisation of Antonio Maria Zaccaria, founder of the Barnabites. Domenichino painted the four cardinal virtues on the pendentives between 1627 and 1630 and Giovanni Lanfranco the apse semi-dome in 1646. Martino Longhi the Younger built the high altar under Borromeo's motto Humilitas, carrying Pietro da Cortona's canvas of Borromeo bearing the Holy Nail in procession during the Milan plague, placed in 1667. There are also works by Mattia and Gregorio Preti on the counter-facade, Lanfranco's Annunciazione of 1624, Giacinto Brandi's Martirio di San Biagio of 1678, Antonio Gherardi's Santa Cecilia, Francesco Romanelli's Martiri Persiani and Andrea Sacchi's Morte di Sant'Anna. The Rieger organ, Opus 600, was built in 1897 to Filippo Capocci's tonal design and restored in 1995 by Angelo Carbonetti.

places.name: Palazzetto del Burcardo
places.summary: A late-Gothic house built between 1491 and 1500 for Johannes Burckardt, the Alsatian bishop and papal master of ceremonies, and the reason Largo di Torre Argentina carries that name. The Biblioteca e Museo teatrale del Burcardo was housed here from 1932; it.wikipedia's rione article records it at this address until February 2017. No current source states whether the building is open, so no opening information is given here.
places.history: Burckardt was born in Alsace between 1445 and 1450, was in Rome from 1467, became papal chaplain in 1478, apostolic protonotary in 1481, master of ceremonies of the papal chapel in 1484 and bishop of Orte and Civita Castellana in 1503, and kept the diary known as the Liber Notarum from 25 December 1484 to 27 April 1506. In 1491 he leased from the abbey of Farfa a piece of ground holding the ruins of a medieval convent with a tower, and built his house around it. The tower he absorbed took the name Argentina from the way he signed himself, episcopus argentinensis, Strasbourg being Argentoratum, and Roma Capitale states on its own Largo di Torre Argentina page that this is where the largo's name comes from.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria in Monterone
places.summary: A basilican church of three naves on antique columns whose Ionic capitals are all different, arranged in the medieval period, recorded in the rione's own monument list. The adjoining convent is now the Redemptorists', who officiate the church. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The church is first recorded among the daughter churches of San Lorenzo in Damaso in a bull of Urban III of 1186. It was restored in 1245 and again in 1597, when it was raised to escape repeated Tiber flooding, and completely rebuilt in 1682 under Innocent XI. The name appears to come from the Monteroni family of Siena, who founded it together with a small hospice for Sienese pilgrims. It was a parish church until Leo XII, 1823 to 1829, transferred the cure of souls to Sant'Eustachio. The high altar carries a Madonna between St Peter Nolasco and St Peter Pascasius by Pompeo Batoni; the funerary monument of Cardinal Stefano Durazzo is on the left presbytery wall, and the Gondi family are buried in the left nave.

places.name: Chiesa di Gesu Nazareno
places.summary: A small church on via dei Barbieri, formerly called de' Filonardi or del Crocifisso and also dedicated to the Most Holy Trinity, which reopened on Christmas night 2012 after years of consolidation and restoration. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: Franciscan tertiaries lived in a house adjoining the church. In the sixteenth century it was entrusted to the guild of barbers, who rebuilt it in 1622 and consecrated it to Ss Cosmas and Damian, and it was almost entirely rebuilt between 1722 and 1724. It was deconsecrated after 1870 and in 1896 granted to the Arciconfraternita di Gesu Nazareno, which gave it its present name. Inside is a Sant'Elena attributed to Pomarancio; a Santa Caterina d'Alessandria by the Cavalier d'Arpino is in the adjoining convent.

places.name: Chiesa evangelica battista di via del Teatro Valle
places.address: Via del Teatro Valle, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A Baptist church still used by a congregation of the UCEBI, its interior painted in Liberty style by Paolo Paschetto, who was a member of the congregation until his death. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The Foreign Mission Board of the Southern Baptist Convention bought a property adjoining the Teatro Valle in 1878, with funds raised among American Baptist congregations, and the church was inaugurated with a service on Sunday 2 November 1878. After 1870 the Board had sent William Nelson Cote to Italy; a Baptist church opened at via della Croce 39 in 1871, but landlords repeatedly moved the community on, and under Georg Boardman Taylor it took a large hall in the former Caffe Cesano at piazza Montecitorio 17 in 1874 and began raising money for a building of its own. The premises had belonged, with the Teatro Valle and Palazzo Capranica alla Valle of 1530, to a single Capranica property running from Piazza Sant'Andrea della Valle to Piazza Sant'Eustachio, and were probably stables or coach houses.

places.name: Palazzo Baldinotti Carpegna
places.summary: A palace adjoining Palazzo Madama, joined to it by a two-storey portico, which houses offices and standing committees of the Senato della Repubblica and belongs to the Senate. It is recorded in the rione's own monument list on corso del Rinascimento, and it is a different building from the Palazzo Carpegna of the Accademia Nazionale di San Luca, which stands in rione Trevi.
places.history: It was built, probably at the end of the seventeenth century, to a design by Giovanni Antonio De Rossi for the Tuscan Baldinotti family, and Cardinal Giovanni Francesco Albani lived here until his election as Clement XI. It passed to the Carpegna by marriage. The Italian State bought it in 1919 and joined it to the Palazzo della Sapienza by a temporary flyover, making it the university's Faculty of Letters and Philosophy. It was partly demolished in 1935 for the cutting of Corso del Rinascimento and then rebuilt on a set-back line.

places.name: Palazzo Mazzetti di Pietralata
places.summary: A neoclassical palace of three storeys and a mezzanine on piazza Rondanini, recorded in the rione's own monument list. The palace is privately owned and is not open to visitors.
places.history: It was built for Don Giovanni Battista Mazzetti, II Marchese di Pietralata, from about 1820, and took roughly fifteen years; the attribution is contested, to Virginio Vespignani by Salvatore Rebecchini and to Giuseppe Marasca by others. It occupies a whole block on four sides as far as Piazza delle Coppelle, and its central courtyard preserves in plan the outline of a large hall of the Terme di Nerone beneath it, together with a stretch of the baths' semicircular wall, as a marble plaque at the secondary staircase records. The elevation is rusticated to the first floor, with a great arched doorway rising to the mezzanine, a Greek-key frieze and a cornice on brackets carrying the family's lion's head, mace and roses. Vincenzo Camuccini frescoed the piano nobile. The family lived here until the 1930s, when the palace was sold.

places.name: Palazzo Patrizi Montoro and the Pinacoteca del Tesoriere
places.summary: A palace still owned by the marchesi Patrizi Naro Montoro, whose piano nobile holds the Pinacoteca del Tesoriere: rooms frescoed by Raffaello Vanni, the family chapel, the Imperial ballroom and a picture collection of about 800 paintings, arranged as it was at the end of the eighteenth century. Roma Capitale places the palace on Piazza di San Luigi de' Francesi. Its address field gives a different street, so no street number is given here. Roma Capitale states that the palace can be visited by booking only.
places.history: The origin is a modest house bought in 1512 by Gaspero dei Garzoni of Jesi from Alfonsina Orsini. In 1605 Olimpia Aldobrandini bought it together with an adjoining building of the Arciconfraternita della Carita and the Ospedale della Consolazione and had the two joined; the facade was finished in 1611. The palace was sold in 1642 to the Patrizi, a Sienese family in Rome from 1537, and through Maria Virginia's marriage in 1726 to Giovanni Chigi Montoro the line became the marchesi Patrizi Naro Montoro. Sebastiano Cipriani altered it in the early eighteenth century, further work followed in 1747, and Luigi Moneti renovated it in 1823. It has three storeys and a mezzanine plus a nineteenth-century addition, and an off-centre portal with two brackets carrying the stars and embattled band of the Aldobrandini arms, repeated on the windows and the cornice.

places.name: Antica Cartotecnica
places.summary: A stationer's on piazza dei Caprettari selling pens, inks, wooden set squares, drafting boards and typewriters. Roma Capitale lists it among the city's historic shops. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that in the 1930s Elisa Berti, grandmother of the present owner, worked at the SACE Cartoleria Esperia, a stationery warehouse supplying ministries, public offices and schools; when the owner gave up the business she took it over as Cartotecnica Commerciale with two other employees, later keeping part of it for herself. Her children Paola and Giovanni joined in the 1950s and shifted the business towards writing instruments, and Eduardo De Filippo and Renato Rascel are named among the customers. Alessandro Billi has run the shop since the 1990s.

entries.name: Chiesa di Sant'Ivo alla Sapienza
entries.note: Borromini's church in the courtyard of the Palazzo della Sapienza, with a six-pointed-star plan and a spiral lantern; the rector's office states that it is closed for works in progress.

entries.name: Chiesa di San Luigi dei Francesi
entries.note: The French national church, whose Contarelli chapel holds the three canvases Caravaggio painted between 1599 and 1602 on the life of St Matthew.

entries.name: Basilica di Sant'Agostino in Campo Marzio
entries.note: Caravaggio's Madonna dei Pellegrini of 1604, Raphael's Prophet Isaiah of 1512 and two Sansovino marbles in one church, raised above a flight of steps.

entries.name: Basilica di Sant'Andrea della Valle
entries.note: Maderno's dome of 1622, frescoed inside by Lanfranco, with Domenichino on the pendentives; open Monday to Saturday 15.00 to 19.30 and Sunday 08.30 to 19.30.

entries.name: Basilica di Sant'Eustachio
entries.note: The church that names the rione, with a stag's head above the pediment, Salvi's altar of 1739 and a plaque marking the Tiber flood of 5 December 1495.

entries.name: Palazzo della Sapienza and the Archivio di Stato di Roma
entries.note: Rome's university sat here from 1303 until 1935; the State Archive has held the building since 1936 and uses the Alessandrina's hall as an exhibition room.

entries.name: Palazzo Madama (Senato della Repubblica)
entries.note: Named for Margherita d'Austria, given its Baroque facade by Marucelli in 1642, and the Senate's seat since February 1871; Roma Capitale states that visits are suspended.

entries.name: Palazzo Giustiniani
entries.note: The Constitution of the Italian Republic was signed in the library room here on 27 December 1947 by President Enrico De Nicola.

entries.name: Teatro Argentina
entries.note: The Teatro di Roma's main house opened on 13 January 1732 with Sarro's Berenice; the 2026/2027 season is running and tickets go through teatrodiroma.vivaticket.it.

entries.name: Teatro Valle "Franca Valeri"
entries.note: A 900-seat house inaugurated on 7 January 1727, reopened in part in 2018 and named for Franca Valeri in 2021, with a published 2026/2027 season.

entries.name: Biblioteca Angelica
entries.note: Angelo Rocca gave his 20,000 volumes to the friars of Sant'Agostino in 1604 and directed that the library be open to all without limit of rank or means.

entries.name: Fontana dei Libri
entries.note: Pietro Lombardi's fountain of 1927 in the flank of the Sapienza: a stag between four books, inscribed with a rione numeral that Roma Capitale says is wrong.

entries.name: Abate Luigi
entries.note: A headless late-Roman statue of a public official, one of the talking statues, standing at the corner of piazza Vidoni since 1924.

entries.name: Antica Cartotecnica
entries.note: Pens, inks, wooden set squares, drafting boards and typewriters on piazza dei Caprettari; Roma Capitale lists it among the city's historic shops.
